introBody:
A student-led marine science organization focused on the biology, ecology, conservation, and responsible field research of sharks.

Our primary research species are the Bluntnose Sixgill Shark, Pacific Spiny Dogfish, and Common Thresher Shark.

Our mission is to build practical research skills, collect reliable observations, expand knowledge of sharks, and promote responsible stewardship of marine ecosystems.

sections.title: Who we are
sections.body:
The Shark Research Club is a student-centered organization for people interested in sharks, marine biology, fisheries science, ecology, conservation, and scientific research.

We combine classroom learning with responsible field observation, research projects, data analysis, and education.
items: Science — Use evidence and reliable sources.
Respect — Treat wild animals and marine habitats responsibly.
Conservation — Use research to improve understanding and stewardship.

sections.title: Three species, many questions
sections.body:
Bluntnose Sixgill Shark — Our primary research species. Its deep-water lifestyle, large size, unusual anatomy, and limited direct observation make it an important subject for scientific study.

Pacific Spiny Dogfish — A coastal shark that provides opportunities to study distribution, schooling behavior, diet, and population patterns.

Common Thresher Shark — A large shark recognized by its exceptionally long upper tail lobe and specialized open-water ecology.

sections.title: A difficult shark to study
sections.body:
The Bluntnose Sixgill Shark (Hexanchus griseus) is a large deep-water shark recognized by six pairs of gill slits, a broad rounded snout, and a single dorsal fin. It is one of the most distinctive large sharks found in the Pacific Northwest.

Much of the sixgill's life occurs in deeper marine environments that are difficult to observe directly. Reliable observations are therefore especially valuable. Sixgills are associated with deep continental shelves and slopes and have been recorded at great depths. They can also occur in coastal and inland marine environments, including parts of the Pacific Northwest.
items: Appearance: six pairs of gill slits, a broad blunt snout, small eyes, a large body, one dorsal fin, and dark brown, gray, or olive coloration.
Size and life history: sixgills can reach approximately 5.5 meters in length. They are long-lived sharks, and females can produce large litters of live young.
Diet: documented prey includes fishes, squid, crustaceans, other sharks, and marine mammals.
Behavior: researchers are still learning how sixgills use different depths and habitats, how their movements change over time, and how behavior relates to environmental conditions.

sections.title: Every observation can add to the bigger picture
sections.body:
The Bluntnose Sixgill Shark is a large, long-lived predator that spends much of its life in environments that are difficult to observe. Many questions about its biology, movement, population structure, and habitat use remain open to research.

Sixgills are predators within marine food webs. Studying their diet, movements, and habitat use can help researchers understand their relationships with prey, competitors, and other predators. Reliable observations can help identify areas where sixgills occur repeatedly, the habitats they use, and changes in their distribution over time.
items: Long-term records can reveal population patterns that a single observation cannot.
Research can examine growth, age structure, maturity, reproduction, juvenile and adult distribution, movement, and longevity.
Movement research can help identify where individuals travel, which depths they use, seasonal changes, and important habitats.
Research can document fisheries interactions and provide information useful to fisheries management.
Better knowledge of distribution, population patterns, habitat, and human impacts supports more informed conservation.

sections.title: From observations to reliable data
sections.body:
Research questions include: Where are sixgills being observed? What sizes and sexes are represented? What habitats are associated with observations? Do observations change seasonally? What can long-term records tell us about local populations?

Research does not always require catching an animal. Photography, video observation, environmental measurements, existing datasets, literature reviews, and remote observations can all contribute to scientific understanding.

Our standard is to collect only information that is necessary for the research question and can be obtained safely and responsibly.
items: Species identification, date and time, and general location.
Size information and sex only when safely obtained or identifiable.

sections.title: Wildlife comes first
sections.body:
A large sixgill shark must be treated as a powerful wild animal. Close interaction can create serious risks for people and stress or injure the shark.

Any capture or handling of a sixgill for research should be performed only by appropriately trained and supervised personnel working under applicable regulations and an established research protocol. The shark's welfare comes before measurements, photographs, or other data.

If you are not trained, do not attempt to handle a sixgill independently. Observe from a safe distance and involve qualified adults or researchers.
items: Plan the activity before it begins and follow applicable laws, permits, and institutional requirements.
Have qualified supervision and keep unnecessary people away from the animal.
Minimize handling and disturbance; treat the mouth, teeth, and entire animal as hazardous.
Avoid unnecessary restraint, lifting, or dragging, and have a release plan before handling begins.

sections.title: Coastal patterns and schooling behavior
sections.body: The Pacific Spiny Dogfish is a smaller shark that can occur in schools along the Pacific coast. Its biology makes it useful for studying distribution, population patterns, feeding ecology, and shark behavior.

sections.title: Open-water ecology
sections.body: The Common Thresher Shark is a large shark recognized by its exceptionally long upper tail lobe. It is associated with open-water environments and has specialized feeding behavior.

sections.title: From observation to data
sections.body:
Good research begins with a clear question, a consistent method, and accurate records. Possible records include species, date, time, general location, environmental conditions, size information when safely available, behavior, and release condition.

Record observations promptly. Clearly separate measured information from estimates and keep methods consistent. Wildlife should never be disturbed simply to obtain a photograph or piece of data. If useful information can be collected without handling an animal, non-invasive observation is preferred.

sections.title: Research, not recreation
sections.body: When capture is part of an authorized scientific project, the objective is to answer a research question while minimizing stress and injury. No measurement, photograph, or research result is more important than the safety and welfare of the animal.
items: Plan before capture and confirm applicable regulations and authorization.
Use trained personnel and minimize handling time.
Prioritize animal welfare and release according to the approved protocol.

sections.title: Science-based stewardship
sections.body:
Sharks play important roles in marine ecosystems. Understanding their populations and habitats helps scientists and resource managers make informed conservation decisions.

Our goal is to promote science-based understanding and responsible stewardship of shark populations and marine habitats.

sections.title: Student research
sections.body:
Members can develop projects based on questions about shark biology, ecology, distribution, behavior, and conservation.

Members learn how to form research questions, find reliable sources, organize data, analyze observations, and communicate scientific results. Our process: Question → Background Research → Data Collection → Analysis → Conclusions → Presentation.
items: Build a local shark observation database.
Analyze published sixgill research and review population studies.
Document habitat conditions and study shark conservation issues.

sections.title: Sharing shark science
sections.body: We want to make shark biology understandable and accurate for students, families, and the broader community. Sharks are complex animals. Understanding them requires evidence, observation, and scientific research—not fear or myths.

sections.title: Join the club
sections.body: You do not need to be an expert to participate. Curiosity and a willingness to learn are the most important requirements. Activities involving wildlife are subject to age-appropriate supervision, safety requirements, applicable laws, and research protocols.
items: Learn shark biology and study scientific research.
Participate in educational projects and practice data recording.
Develop research skills and explore marine science careers.

sections.title: Build better research
sections.body:
Members are encouraged to use peer-reviewed research, universities, government agencies, museums, aquariums, and established scientific organizations.

Evaluate your sources: ask who published the information, what evidence supports it, when it was published, and whether reliable sources agree. Good science depends on reliable sources, careful observation, transparent methods, and accurate records.
